evidence_quotes.quote: A large factorial field experiment in Mumbai’s informal settlements reveals that a bureaucratic facilitation drive significantly improved citizens’ ability to access municipal water connections in policy-eligible settlements, but only when combined with a bottom-up political coordination campaign targeting elected officials.
Gathering required documents such as proof-of-address certifications, licensed plumbers’ approvals, and evidence of slums’ legal status.
Liaising with authorities to negotiate eligibility rules, documentation requirements, and ancillary permissions.

While settlements on many types of land faced significant bureaucratic hurdles when it came to obtaining legal water supply from the BMC, there were settlements on three specific types of land—footpaths, forest, and salt pan land—that faced legal and policy barriers that made it impossible for them to get official municipal connections without a change in the existing policy or legal framework.
Our experimental sample comprises 153 slum clusters, which were demarcated during a mapping exercise carried out before the baseline survey.
Table 1 reports the estimated effect of our interventions, as well as their interaction, on “full formalization”—that is, access to a verified municipal water connection.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to formal municipal piped water connections (Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation group standpost connections) in informal settlements (slums) in Mumbai, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines bureaucratic, legal, policy, and political governance factors shaping municipal water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study directly tests and analyzes multiple rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) administrative burden, application procedures, and documentation requirements via Treatment 1 (bureaucratic facilitation with group formation, proof-of-address certifications, evidence of slums' legal status, licensed plumbers' approvals, online portal submission, RTI requests, and negotiating eligibility and documentation rules); (2) formal legal and policy eligibility exclusions by land tenure/category under the 2014 Bombay High Court judgment, 2017 BMC water policy, and court orders barring connections on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands; and (3) bureaucratic and political discretion around multi-agency land-use No Objection Certificates (NOCs) and P-form approvals, interacted with Treatment 2 (bottom-up political coordination).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative and qualitative empirical evidence from a pre-registered multi-level factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial across 76 slums (152 analyzed slum clusters; N = 6,268 at midline in 2019 and N = 6,652 at endline in 2023), supplemented by semi-structured qualitative interviews and NGO field reports.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household-level water access and connection outcomes, primarily 'full formalization' (enumerator-verified BMC municipal water pipe connection and meter acquired post-intervention) as well as intermediate formalization stages (official application submitted, BMC engineer inspection visit, P-form permission received, and a 0-3 ordinal formalization scale).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (unconnected households nested within slum clusters and slums in Mumbai, with weighted least squares estimation clustered at the slum cluster or slum level), the randomized exposures and legal/administrative moderators, the verified connection outcomes, and the factorial cluster-RCT study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Multi-level 2x2 factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial (field experiment) with midline (1-year) and endline (5-year) household surveys, supplemented by qualitative semi-structured interviews and NGO field reports.
population_and_sample: Households lacking formal municipal water connections in informal settlements (slums) in Mumbai, India: 76 slums (153 mapped slum clusters; 152 randomized and analyzed clusters; 48 policy-eligible slums / 116 clusters and 28 policy-ineligible slums / 36 clusters), with N = 6,268 household respondents at midline (2019) and N = 6,652 household respondents at endline (2023, including replacement sample; N = 5,251 in the eligible lands sample).
exposure: Factorial randomization of Treatment 1 (door-to-door bureaucratic assistance reducing administrative burden, proof-of-address/slum-status documentation hurdles, and online application barriers at the slum-cluster level) and Treatment 2 (collective political coordination and petitioning targeting elected officials and bureaucrats at the slum level), analyzed across legal/policy land-eligibility regimes (eligible lands vs. footpath, forest, and salt pan lands excluded by BMC policy and court orders) and land-authority No Objection Certificate (NOC) requirements.
outcome: Household acquisition of a formal, enumerator-verified Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) piped water connection with meter ('full formalization') at 5-year endline, plus intermediate formalization stages at 1-year midline and endline (application submission, BMC inspection visit, P-form approval, and 0-3 ordinal formalization level).
rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Gaikwad & Thomas, 'Getting on the Grid: A Field Experiment on Bottom-Up Political Pressure and Access to Essential Public Services'). The study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It is a pre-registered factorial cluster-randomized field experiment in Mumbai's informal settlements examining how relieving household administrative and documentation burdens (proof-of-address, legal status documentation, licensed plumber sign-off, online portal filing, and negotiating eligibility rules), combined with bottom-up political pressure to overcome bureaucratic/political discretion in land-authority No Objection Certificate (NOC) clearances and bounded by formal legal/policy land-eligibility exclusions (2014 Bombay High Court ruling, 2017 BMC policy, and court orders on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands), affects verified household municipal piped water connections.
